title: How to Think Like a Leader Before You Feel Like One
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Chiarelli's premise is that leadership is a practice, and practices can be learned through deliberate action even if you do not yet feel like the person who does them. The argument is against waiting for confidence: the old story is that you feel confident first and then act. The newer research suggests the opposite. You act first, consistently, in alignment with the role you want to occupy. That repeated action reshapes your identity. The practical implication is that you do not need to feel like a leader to start thinking like one. You make the decision to prepare more thoroughly for a meeting, to ask better questions, to acknowledge what you do not know, to keep your word on small things, to listen to people you disagree with. Each of those actions is a leadership move. Do them repeatedly and the felt sense of leadership follows. Chiarelli is careful to name that this is not faking it; it is honouring the person you are becoming by acting like that person before the identity has fully settled. It is a practical rebuttal to the idea that authenticity means waiting until you feel ready.
points: Leadership is a practice; you learn it through deliberate action, not through waiting for confidence or feeling.

Identity follows repeated action; make leadership moves (prepare thoroughly, ask better questions, acknowledge ignorance, keep your word, listen to disagreement) and the felt sense of leadership follows.
This is not faking it; it is honouring the person you are becoming by acting like that person before the identity has fully settled.
quotes: Early in my career I felt that credibility came from speed and execution. Clients asked a question; I raced to answer. Teams brought a problem; I offered a fix. As I took on leadership roles, I realised that (1) I didn't have time to be a doer in the same way; and (2) it was no longer my job to do so! Instead of acting and effectively closing spaces that others could own, I had to provide the space for others to think for themselves.

My natural instinct was (and still is!) to sketch a solution. Instead, I asked, “What would success look like if we got this right?” The room went quiet for a few seconds. Then, ideas started to surface: hesitant at first, then layered and richer. Within twenty minutes they had built a vision none of us could have produced alone.
Holding a question like in this example doesn't mean being evasive or lacking confidence. It means resisting the reflex to perform knowledge and instead creating a space for shared sense-making.

When I first stepped into leadership roles, I thought the job was to push. Push projects forward, push performance, push for change. It took me a while to realise that most people and teams actually struggle because something is slowing them down.

Leadership, I've learned, is often about identifying and removing these hidden barriers. You can spot them by paying attention to what hinders colleagues: unclear roles, competing expectations, unspoken conflict, fragmented processes, interpersonal tensions that people are worried they can't voice.

One of the hardest transitions in leadership is realising that your internal weather becomes everyone else's climate. You may think you're having a private moment of frustration, but people feel the shift instantly. Tone, posture, speed of speech — teams track these cues far more than we imagine.

My irritation didn't stay contained. It set the emotional baseline, and the meeting shifted toward managing the tension I had brought into the room. We spent the next hour dealing with the consequences of a mood swing rather than the substance of the work.

A leadership mindset is the craft of shaping the conditions under which good thinking, good work and good relationships can emerge. … Together, these practices shift leadership from performance to stewardship: you are not trying to be impressive, but to be useful.” Archived from Andrea Chiarelli on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
